procedural_history.impugned_order: Common order acquitting several accused persons at a joint trial.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State filed a joint appeal against the respondents (accused) in the Gujarat High Court (Criminal Appeals Nos. 951 and 796 of 1963). A Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the joint appeal, holding that such an appeal was not maintainable. The Division Bench considered itself not bound by a prior Full Bench decision of the same court (in Lallu Jida's case) which had taken a contrary view.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeals Nos. 60 and 63 of 1965). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remitted the case back to the High Court for a decision on the merits of the appeal. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was wrong in holding the joint appeal not maintainable and in summarily rejecting it, and that the Division Bench was in error in not treating the earlier decision of a Full Bench of the same court on the same question as binding.

directions: Set aside the order of the High Court.
Remit the case back to the High Court for decision of the appeal on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether a single joint appeal by the State is maintainable against a common order of acquittal of several accused persons who were jointly tried.

facts: The State filed a single, joint appeal against several accused persons who were acquitted in a joint trial by a common order.
The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that a joint appeal was not maintainable under the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
law: The relevant provisions considered were Sections 258, 410, 417, 419, and 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Court also considered, by analogy, Rule 6 of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, which allows multiple persons aggrieved by the same criminal judgment to join in one appeal.
application: The Supreme Court examined the specified sections of the Cr.P.C. and found that none of them contained any provision that prohibited a joint appeal by the State.
The Court specifically interpreted Section 417, noting that it provides for an appeal "in a case" and not against a specific accused person, making its language wide enough to permit a joint appeal.
It rejected the High Court's view that Section 419, which deals with the form of an appeal petition, created a bar against a joint appeal.

The Court reasoned by analogy, stating that if multiple convicted persons can file a joint appeal (as permitted by court rules), then on principle, the State should also be able to file a single appeal against multiple acquitted persons from the same joint trial.

The Court characterized the issue as a matter of procedure, not substantive rights. It stated that procedure is the "hand-maid and not a mistress of law" and should be interpreted liberally to facilitate justice, not obstruct it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a single joint appeal by the State against several accused persons acquitted by a common order is maintainable. It found no legal bar in the Code of Criminal Procedure and held that since the matter is one of form, a liberal approach should be taken to hear the appeal on its merits in the interest of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Division Bench of a High Court is bound by an earlier decision of a Full Bench of the same court on the same legal question.

facts: A Division Bench of a High Court was faced with the question of whether a joint appeal by the State against several acquitted persons was maintainable.
An earlier Full Bench of the same High Court, in a case known as *Lalu Jela's case*, had already decided this question, holding that such an appeal was maintainable.
The Division Bench disagreed with the Full Bench's reasoning and concluded that the Full Bench decision was not binding on it.
Consequently, the Division Bench dismissed the State's joint appeal as not maintainable.
law: The Supreme Court referenced its prior ruling in *Mahadeolal Kanodia v. The Administrator General of West Bengal*.

This precedent establishes that for reasons of judicial decorum, legal propriety, and the need for certainty in law, judges of co-ordinate jurisdiction in a High Court should not overrule one another's decisions.
If a bench disagrees with an earlier decision of a co-ordinate bench, the proper procedure is to refer the question to a larger bench.
Allowing benches to overrule each other would lead to "utter confusion" and destroy the quality of certainty in law.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle from *Mahadeolal Kanodia* to the current case.
It found that the Division Bench acted improperly by taking it upon itself to declare the previous Full Bench decision wrong.
Instead of following the established procedure of referring the matter to a larger bench due to its difference of opinion, the Division Bench simply disregarded the binding precedent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Division Bench was in error for not treating the earlier decision of the Full Bench as binding. A Division Bench is bound by a prior decision of a Full Bench of the same court on the same legal question.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a single joint appeal by the State is maintainable against a common order of acquittal of several accused persons who were jointly tried.
appellant_arguments: The relevant sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), including sections 258, 410, 417, 419, and 423, do not prohibit a joint appeal by the State.
Section 417 allows for an appeal 'in a case', not just against an individual accused person, which is wide enough to permit a joint appeal.
On principle, if multiple convicted persons can file a joint appeal, the State should be able to file a joint appeal against a common order of acquittal.
The rules for filing an appeal are procedural matters intended to facilitate justice, not obstruct it. Holding a joint appeal as unmaintainable would defeat the cause of justice.
respondent_arguments: The respondents were unrepresented in the Supreme Court. However, the High Court, whose decision was being appealed, had argued that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Cr.P.C., and particularly Section 419, is against the maintainability of a joint appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Division Bench of a High Court is bound by an earlier decision of a Full Bench of the same court on the same legal question.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument is implicit: The Division Bench erred by not following the binding precedent set by the Full Bench of the same court, which had already decided the issue of the maintainability of a joint appeal.
respondent_arguments: The respondents were unrepresented. The Division Bench of the High Court, however, had argued at length that the earlier Full Bench decision was not binding on it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A joint appeal by the State against several accused persons who were jointly tried and acquitted by a common order is maintainable and not legally prohibited, as this is a matter of procedure intended to facilitate the cause of justice.
obiter: If a Division Bench of a High Court disagrees with a previous decision of another Division Bench, it should not overrule it but should refer the question to a larger Bench to ensure legal certainty and uphold judicial decorum.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that a single joint appeal by the State against a common order acquitting several accused persons is maintainable, as it is not prohibited by the Code of Criminal Procedure and is supported by procedural fairness. The Court also found that the High Court's Division Bench committed a clear error by failing to follow a binding precedent set by a Full Bench of the same court, a practice which undermines the necessary quality of certainty in law.
legal_tests_applied: Stare Decisis / Binding Precedent: The Court applied the principle that a Division Bench is bound by the decision of a Full Bench of the same court. The Court stated, 'The Division Bench was in error in not treating as binding the earlier decision of a Full Bench of the same court on the same question.' The proper procedure in case of disagreement is 'referring the question to a larger Bench,' not for judges of co-ordinate jurisdiction to overrule one another.

Statutory Interpretation of the Code of Criminal Procedure: The Court analyzed the relevant sections and found no prohibition against a joint appeal. It reasoned that Section 417 'provides for an appeal in a case, and not against an accused person, who has been acquitted. The plain reading of this section. therefore, seems to he wide enough to permit a joint appeal.' It further found that Section 419 'does not seem to us to prohibit a joint appeal by the State against more than one accused perso11~.'

Reasoning by Analogy: The Court reasoned that if convicted persons can file a joint appeal, the State should have a reciprocal right. 'if an appeal by persons jointly tried and convicted is competent, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability of one appeal by the State against a common order acquitting several persons tried jointly.'
policy_considerations: Promotion of Justice over Procedural Technicalities: The Court emphasized that procedure must serve justice, stating, 'Proccdu1:e has been described to be a hand-maid and not a mistress of law, intended to subserve und faciUtate the cause of justice and not to govern or obstruct it.' Holding the appeal unmaintainable on a procedural ground 'wouM defeat the larger cause of justice.'

Certainty and Judicial Decorum: The Court stressed the importance of consistency and predictability in law. 'Judicial decorum no less than legal propriety forms the basis.of judicial procedure. If one thing is more necessary in law than any other thing, it is the quality of certainty. That quality would totally disappear if jud-ges of co-ordinate jurisdiction in a High Court start over-ruling one another's decision.'
